::: callout-note
## In this session you will learn to

1.  Explain the three parts every ggplot needs: data, aesthetics (`aes()`), and a geometry (`geom_`)
2.  Make histograms, scatter plots, and box plots
3.  Tell the difference between **mapping** a variable to color and **setting** a fixed color
4.  Add titles, axis labels, and a theme

**Before you start:** open the workshop folder in Positron (**File → Open Folder...**) and open `student_scripts/Session 6 - Plotting Basics_STUDENT.R`. This session starts from `combined_linelist.rds` and `measles_final.rds`, the files you saved in Session 3. If you missed it, ready-made copies are already in the `processed_data/` folder.
:::

# Part 1: Set up


::: {.cell}

```{.r .cell-code}
library(tidyverse)
library(here)
library(rio)

linelist <- import(here("processed_data", "combined_linelist.rds"), trust = TRUE) %>%
  mutate(
    age_cat = fct_relevel(age_cat, "Under 18", "18-29", "30-39", "40-49",
                          "50-59", "60-69", "70-79", "80+", "Unknown"),
    outcome = fct_relevel(outcome, "Recover", "Death", "Unknown")
  )
```
:::


The factor order from Session 5 isn't saved in the file, so we set it again right after importing.

::: {.callout-important .tryit icon=false}
## ✏️ TRY IT (3 min): import and order the measles data

Import `measles_final.rds` as `measles` and `fct_relevel()` `age_cat` ("Under 5", "5-9", "10-14", "15+", "Unknown") and `vaccinated` ("Yes", "No", "Unknown"), in one pipeline.

✅ **Check:** `levels(measles$age_cat)` starts with "Under 5"

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" icon=false}
## Show solution


::: {.cell}

```{.r .cell-code}
measles <- import(here("processed_data", "measles_final.rds"), trust = TRUE) %>%
  mutate(
    age_cat    = fct_relevel(age_cat, "Under 5", "5-9", "10-14", "15+", "Unknown"),
    vaccinated = fct_relevel(vaccinated, "Yes", "No", "Unknown")
  )

levels(measles$age_cat)
```

::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout}

```
[1] "Under 5" "5-9"     "10-14"   "15+"     "Unknown"
```


:::
:::


`import()` and `mutate()` are joined by the pipe, so the data is imported and put in order in one step. Plots will now show the age groups and vaccination status in this order.
:::
:::

# Part 2: The grammar of graphics

Every ggplot is built from the same parts, added together with `+`:

| Part            | Function    | Question it answers                        |
|-----------------|-------------|--------------------------------------------|
| **Data**        | `ggplot(data = ...)` | Which data frame?                 |
| **Aesthetics**  | `aes()`     | Which columns go on x, y, color, fill, ...? |
| **Geometry**    | `geom_...()` | What shape: bars, points, boxes, lines?   |
| Labels          | `labs()`    | Title and axis names                       |
| Theme           | `theme_...()` | The overall look                         |

Build it up one piece at a time, and run the code after every `+` so you can see what each layer adds:


::: {.cell}

```{.r .cell-code}
# 1. Data only: an empty canvas
ggplot(data = linelist)
```

::: {.cell-output-display}
![](06-plotting-basics_files/figure-html/unnamed-chunk-3-1.png){width=672}
:::
:::



::: {.cell}

```{.r .cell-code}
# 2. Add aesthetics: the axes appear, but nothing is drawn yet
ggplot(data = linelist, mapping = aes(x = age_years))
```

::: {.cell-output-display}
![](06-plotting-basics_files/figure-html/unnamed-chunk-4-1.png){width=672}
:::
:::



::: {.cell}

```{.r .cell-code}
# 3. Add a geometry: now we have a plot
ggplot(data = linelist, mapping = aes(x = age_years)) +
  geom_histogram()
```

::: {.cell-output-display}
![](06-plotting-basics_files/figure-html/unnamed-chunk-5-1.png){width=672}
:::
:::


::: callout-important
## `+` not `%>%`

Layers of a ggplot are joined with `+`. Using `%>%` between ggplot layers is the most common beginner error. Like the pipe, `+` goes at the **end** of a line, not the start of the next one.
:::

::: {.callout-important .tryit icon=false}
## ✏️ TRY IT (2 min): build a plot in three steps

Build a histogram of `measles` `temp_c` in the same three steps: data, then `aes()`, then `geom_histogram()`.

✅ **Check:** step 2 shows an empty plot with temperatures on the x-axis

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" icon=false}
## Show solution


::: {.cell}

```{.r .cell-code}
ggplot(data = measles)
```

::: {.cell-output-display}
![](06-plotting-basics_files/figure-html/unnamed-chunk-6-1.png){width=672}
:::

```{.r .cell-code}
ggplot(data = measles, mapping = aes(x = temp_c))
```

::: {.cell-output-display}
![](06-plotting-basics_files/figure-html/unnamed-chunk-6-2.png){width=672}
:::

```{.r .cell-code}
ggplot(data = measles, mapping = aes(x = temp_c)) +
  geom_histogram()
```

::: {.cell-output-display}
![](06-plotting-basics_files/figure-html/unnamed-chunk-6-3.png){width=672}
:::
:::


Step 1 is a blank canvas, step 2 adds the temperature axis, and only step 3 (the geometry) draws the bars.
:::
:::

# Part 3: Histograms

A histogram shows the **distribution** of one number: the values are grouped into ranges ("bins"), and each bar's height is how many values fall in that range.

R warned us above that it picked 30 bins. Choose the bin width yourself:


::: {.cell}

```{.r .cell-code}
ggplot(data = linelist, mapping = aes(x = age_years)) +
  geom_histogram(binwidth = 5)
```

::: {.cell-output-display}
![](06-plotting-basics_files/figure-html/unnamed-chunk-7-1.png){width=672}
:::
:::


Each bar is now 5 years wide. Try `binwidth = 1` and `binwidth = 10` — what changes?

## Fixed colors

Inside `geom_histogram()`, `fill` is the inside color and `color` is the outline. A white outline separates the bars.


::: {.cell}

```{.r .cell-code}
ggplot(data = linelist, mapping = aes(x = age_years)) +
  geom_histogram(binwidth = 5, fill = "#2a78d6", color = "white")
```

::: {.cell-output-display}
![](06-plotting-basics_files/figure-html/unnamed-chunk-8-1.png){width=672}
:::
:::


::: callout-note
## Colors in R

Use a name (`"steelblue"`, `"gray50"`) or a hex code (`"#2a78d6"`). Run `colors()` to see all 657 named colors.
:::

::: {.callout-important .tryit icon=false}
## ✏️ TRY IT (3 min): measles ages

Make a histogram of `measles` `age_years` with `binwidth = 1`, a fill color, and a white outline. Which age has the most cases?

✅ **Check:** the tallest bar is at age 2 (about 100 cases). The warning about "removed rows" is the 29 missing ages: that's fine.

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" icon=false}
## Show solution


::: {.cell}

```{.r .cell-code}
ggplot(data = measles, mapping = aes(x = age_years)) +
  geom_histogram(binwidth = 1, fill = "#2a78d6", color = "white")
```

::: {.cell-output-display}
![](06-plotting-basics_files/figure-html/unnamed-chunk-9-1.png){width=672}
:::
:::


The tallest bar is age 2 (102 cases), and most cases are ages 1–5. ggplot can't draw the 29 rows with a missing age, so it drops them and tells you.
:::
:::

# Part 4: Mapping vs setting

This is the key idea of ggplot:

-   **Mapping** — *inside* `aes()`: a **column** controls the color. Different values get different colors, and you get a legend.
-   **Setting** — *outside* `aes()`: one **fixed** color for everything.


::: {.cell}

```{.r .cell-code}
# Mapping: fill depends on the outcome column
ggplot(data = linelist, mapping = aes(x = age_years, fill = outcome)) +
  geom_histogram(binwidth = 5, color = "white")
```

::: {.cell-output-display}
![](06-plotting-basics_files/figure-html/unnamed-chunk-10-1.png){width=672}
:::
:::



::: {.cell}

```{.r .cell-code}
# Setting: every bar is blue
ggplot(data = linelist, mapping = aes(x = age_years)) +
  geom_histogram(binwidth = 5, fill = "#2a78d6", color = "white")
```

::: {.cell-output-display}
![](06-plotting-basics_files/figure-html/unnamed-chunk-11-1.png){width=672}
:::
:::


::: {.callout-note collapse="true" icon=false}
## 🤔 Think about it: what happens if you put `fill = "blue"` *inside* `aes()`? Try it!


::: {.cell}

```{.r .cell-code}
ggplot(data = linelist, mapping = aes(x = age_years, fill = "blue")) +
  geom_histogram(binwidth = 5)
```

::: {.cell-output-display}
![](06-plotting-basics_files/figure-html/unnamed-chunk-12-1.png){width=672}
:::
:::


The bars are pink-red and the legend says "blue"! ggplot treated "blue" as data — a column whose every value is the word "blue" — and gave it the first default color.
:::

::: callout-warning
## Common mistakes

-   `aes(fill = "blue")` does **not** make blue bars. To use one fixed color, put `fill = "blue"` in the `geom_...()`, outside `aes()`.
:::

::: {.callout-important .tryit icon=false}
## ✏️ TRY IT (3 min): mapping fill

Make a histogram of `measles` `temp_c` with `binwidth = 0.2`, then map `fill = fever` inside `aes()`. Why are there two "humps"?

✅ **Check:** the small hump near 37 °C is "no" fever; the big one near 39 °C is "yes"

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" icon=false}
## Show solution


::: {.cell}

```{.r .cell-code}
ggplot(data = measles, mapping = aes(x = temp_c)) +
  geom_histogram(binwidth = 0.2, color = "white")
```

::: {.cell-output-display}
![](06-plotting-basics_files/figure-html/unnamed-chunk-13-1.png){width=672}
:::

```{.r .cell-code}
ggplot(data = measles, mapping = aes(x = temp_c, fill = fever)) +
  geom_histogram(binwidth = 0.2, color = "white")
```

::: {.cell-output-display}
![](06-plotting-basics_files/figure-html/unnamed-chunk-13-2.png){width=672}
:::
:::


The small hump near 37 °C is the 99 patients without fever; the big hump near 39 °C is the 1064 patients with fever. Mapping `fill` to `fever` shows that the two humps are two groups.
:::
:::

# Part 5: Scatter plots

A scatter plot shows the **relationship** between two numbers: one point per row.


::: {.cell}

```{.r .cell-code}
ggplot(data = linelist, mapping = aes(x = age_years, y = wt_kg)) +
  geom_point()
```

::: {.cell-output-display}
![](06-plotting-basics_files/figure-html/unnamed-chunk-14-1.png){width=672}
:::
:::


With 6,000+ points, many sit on top of each other. Make them smaller and see-through with `size` and `alpha` (0 = invisible, 1 = solid):


::: {.cell}

```{.r .cell-code}
ggplot(data = linelist, mapping = aes(x = age_years, y = wt_kg)) +
  geom_point(size = 1, alpha = 0.3)
```

::: {.cell-output-display}
![](06-plotting-basics_files/figure-html/unnamed-chunk-15-1.png){width=672}
:::
:::


## Map a third variable to color


::: {.cell}

```{.r .cell-code}
ggplot(data = linelist, mapping = aes(x = age_years, y = wt_kg, color = gender)) +
  geom_point(size = 1, alpha = 0.4)
```

::: {.cell-output-display}
![](06-plotting-basics_files/figure-html/unnamed-chunk-16-1.png){width=672}
:::
:::


## Add a trend line

`geom_smooth()` adds a trend line on top of the points. `method = "lm"` draws a straight line (linear model); `se = FALSE` hides the confidence band.


::: {.cell}

```{.r .cell-code}
ggplot(data = linelist, mapping = aes(x = age_years, y = wt_kg)) +
  geom_point(size = 1, alpha = 0.3) +
  geom_smooth(method = "lm", se = FALSE, color = "#eb6834")
```

::: {.cell-output-display}
![](06-plotting-basics_files/figure-html/unnamed-chunk-17-1.png){width=672}
:::
:::


## Filter right inside `ggplot()`

You can pipe data into `ggplot()`, so you can `filter()` first without making a new object:


::: {.cell}

```{.r .cell-code}
linelist %>%
  filter(fever == "yes") %>%
  ggplot(mapping = aes(x = age_years, y = wt_kg)) +
  geom_point(size = 1, alpha = 0.3)
```

::: {.cell-output-display}
![](06-plotting-basics_files/figure-html/unnamed-chunk-18-1.png){width=672}
:::
:::


Notice the switch: `%>%` **into** `ggplot()`, then `+` **between** layers.

::: {.callout-important .tryit icon=false}
## ✏️ TRY IT (4 min): a scatter plot

For hospitalized patients only (`filter(!is.na(days_in_hospital))`), plot `age_years` (x) against `days_in_hospital` (y) with `alpha`, and add a trend line. Is there a relationship?

✅ **Check:** 427 hospitalized patients; the trend line is almost flat (no relationship)

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" icon=false}
## Show solution


::: {.cell}

```{.r .cell-code}
measles %>%
  filter(!is.na(days_in_hospital)) %>%
  ggplot(mapping = aes(x = age_years, y = days_in_hospital)) +
  geom_point(alpha = 0.3) +
  geom_smooth(method = "lm", se = FALSE, color = "#eb6834")
```

::: {.cell-output-display}
![](06-plotting-basics_files/figure-html/unnamed-chunk-19-1.png){width=672}
:::
:::


The trend line is almost flat: older and younger patients stay in hospital about as long. "No relationship" is a result too!
:::
:::

# Part 6: Box plots

A box plot compares the **distribution of a number across groups**:

-   The thick line is the **median**
-   The box holds the middle 50% of values (from the 25th to the 75th percentile — the **IQR**)
-   The whiskers reach the most extreme values within 1.5 × IQR of the box
-   Points beyond the whiskers are possible **outliers**


::: {.cell}

```{.r .cell-code}
ggplot(data = linelist, mapping = aes(x = gender, y = age_years)) +
  geom_boxplot()
```

::: {.cell-output-display}
![](06-plotting-basics_files/figure-html/unnamed-chunk-20-1.png){width=672}
:::
:::


## Clean it up

Remove the "Unknown" group, color the boxes, and drop the legend (the x-axis already names the groups):


::: {.cell}

```{.r .cell-code}
linelist %>%
  filter(gender != "Unknown") %>%
  ggplot(mapping = aes(x = gender, y = age_years, fill = gender)) +
  geom_boxplot() +
  theme(legend.position = "none")
```

::: {.cell-output-display}
![](06-plotting-basics_files/figure-html/unnamed-chunk-21-1.png){width=672}
:::
:::


## Add the mean

`stat_summary()` calculates a statistic for each group and draws it. Here, the mean as a diamond:


::: {.cell}

```{.r .cell-code}
linelist %>%
  filter(gender != "Unknown") %>%
  ggplot(mapping = aes(x = gender, y = age_years, fill = gender)) +
  geom_boxplot() +
  stat_summary(fun = mean, geom = "point", shape = 23, size = 3, fill = "white") +
  theme(legend.position = "none")
```

::: {.cell-output-display}
![](06-plotting-basics_files/figure-html/unnamed-chunk-22-1.png){width=672}
:::
:::


::: {.callout-note collapse="true" icon=false}
## 🤔 Think about it: why is the mean (diamond) above the median (line)?

The ages are right-skewed: a few older patients pull the mean up. For example, the median age of female cases is 11 but the mean is 12.7.
:::

::: callout-note
`geom_violin()` shows the full shape of each distribution. Try swapping it in for `geom_boxplot()`.
:::

::: {.callout-important .tryit icon=false}
## ✏️ TRY IT (4 min): a box plot

Make a box plot of `days_in_hospital` by `vaccinated` (hospitalized patients only), with the mean and no legend.

✅ **Check:** three boxes; the medians are 4–5 days for every group

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" icon=false}
## Show solution


::: {.cell}

```{.r .cell-code}
measles %>%
  filter(!is.na(days_in_hospital)) %>%
  ggplot(mapping = aes(x = vaccinated, y = days_in_hospital, fill = vaccinated)) +
  geom_boxplot() +
  stat_summary(fun = mean, geom = "point", shape = 23, size = 3, fill = "white") +
  theme(legend.position = "none")
```

::: {.cell-output-display}
![](06-plotting-basics_files/figure-html/unnamed-chunk-23-1.png){width=672}
:::
:::


The medians are 4 days (Yes) and 5 days (No, Unknown), and the means are all about 5: no clear difference in hospital stay by vaccination status. The boxes appear in the order you set with `fct_relevel()` in Part 1.
:::
:::

# Part 7: Labels and themes

## `labs()`


::: {.cell}

```{.r .cell-code}
linelist %>%
  filter(gender != "Unknown") %>%
  ggplot(mapping = aes(x = gender, y = age_years, fill = gender)) +
  geom_boxplot() +
  labs(
    title    = "Age distribution by gender",
    subtitle = "Cases with known gender",
    x        = "Gender",
    y        = "Age (years)",
    caption  = "Source: workshop outbreak linelist"
  ) +
  theme(legend.position = "none")
```

::: {.cell-output-display}
![](06-plotting-basics_files/figure-html/unnamed-chunk-24-1.png){width=672}
:::
:::


## Themes

A theme changes the look of everything that isn't data: background, grid lines, fonts. Try `theme_minimal()`, `theme_classic()`, `theme_bw()`, and `theme_light()`.


::: {.cell}

```{.r .cell-code}
ggplot(data = linelist, mapping = aes(x = age_years)) +
  geom_histogram(binwidth = 5, fill = "#2a78d6", color = "white") +
  labs(
    title = "Age distribution of cases",
    x     = "Age (years)",
    y     = "Number of cases"
  ) +
  theme_minimal(base_size = 14)
```

::: {.cell-output-display}
![](06-plotting-basics_files/figure-html/unnamed-chunk-25-1.png){width=672}
:::
:::


`base_size` makes all the text bigger — useful for slides.

::: callout-warning
## Order matters

A complete theme like `theme_minimal()` resets everything, so put it **before** `theme(legend.position = ...)` or your change will be overwritten.
:::

## Save a plot as an object

A plot can be saved with `<-` and built on later:


::: {.cell}

```{.r .cell-code}
age_plot <- ggplot(data = linelist, mapping = aes(x = age_years)) +
  geom_histogram(binwidth = 5, fill = "#2a78d6", color = "white")

age_plot +
  labs(title = "Age distribution of cases", x = "Age (years)", y = "Number of cases") +
  theme_minimal()
```

::: {.cell-output-display}
![](06-plotting-basics_files/figure-html/unnamed-chunk-26-1.png){width=672}
:::
:::


::: {.callout-important .tryit icon=false}
## ✏️ TRY IT (5 min): finish a plot

Finish one of your measles plots with a title, subtitle, axis labels, a caption, and a theme. Save it as `my_plot`.

✅ **Check:** typing `my_plot` in the Console shows your finished plot

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" icon=false}
## Show solution


::: {.cell}

```{.r .cell-code}
my_plot <- ggplot(data = measles, mapping = aes(x = temp_c, fill = fever)) +
  geom_histogram(binwidth = 0.2, color = "white") +
  labs(
    title    = "Temperature of measles cases",
    subtitle = "Patients with fever cluster around 39 °C",
    x        = "Temperature (°C)",
    y        = "Number of cases",
    fill     = "Fever",
    caption  = "Source: practice measles linelist"
  ) +
  theme_minimal()

my_plot
```

::: {.cell-output-display}
![](06-plotting-basics_files/figure-html/unnamed-chunk-27-1.png){width=672}
:::
:::


This is one example — any measles plot works. `fill = "Fever"` inside `labs()` renames the legend title. Saving the plot as `my_plot` stores it in the **Variables** pane, and typing its name draws it.
:::
:::

::: callout-tip
## ⭐ Bonus

1.  Make the measles age histogram with `fill = vaccinated`. Which ages have the most unvaccinated cases?
2.  Swap `geom_boxplot()` for `geom_violin()` in your box plot. What does it show?
3.  Brought your own data? Make a histogram, a scatter plot, and a box plot.

See the solutions file for the code.
:::

# Key points

-   Every ggplot needs **data**, **aesthetics** (`aes()`), and a **geometry** (`geom_...()`); layers are joined with `+`, not `%>%`.
-   `geom_histogram()` shows the distribution of one number — choose the `binwidth` yourself.
-   **Mapping** (inside `aes()`) lets a column control color and adds a legend; **setting** (outside `aes()`) uses one fixed color.
-   `geom_point()` shows the relationship between two numbers; `alpha` and `size` help with overlapping points, and `geom_smooth(method = "lm")` adds a trend line.
-   `geom_boxplot()` compares a number across groups; `stat_summary()` adds the mean.
-   `labs()` adds titles and axis labels, and a complete theme like `theme_minimal()` changes the overall look (put it before `theme(...)` changes).
-   You can pipe data into `ggplot()` to `filter()` first, and save a plot as an object with `<-`.

**Next: Session 7 — Plotting further.** We make bar charts, choose colors, draw epidemic curves, split plots into facets, and save plots to files.
